Forbes Staff.

Mary Roeloffs is a Forbes breaking news reporter covering pop culture.

## Topline

Iranian forces appear to have seized a tanker owned by Greek shipping magnate George Prokopiou after striking it in the Strait of Hormuz, part of a wave of attacks that has effectively halted commercial traffic through one of the world's most important oil transit routes.

Ships are docked along a pier at the Khor Fakkan Container Terminal along the Gulf of Oman on July 14, 2026.

# Security concerns continue to linger as the number of vessels crossing Hormuz falls further

Posted to [Maritime Reporter](/blogs/blogs-maritime_reporter)
on
July 22, 2026

Shipping data revealed that vessel crossings through the Strait of Hormuz dropped further on Tuesday as security concerns persisted amid the ongoing attacks by the United States and Iran.

Kpler data shows that on Tuesday only a total of?of?three cargo vessels crossed the Strait, compared to four the day before.

Kpler data showed that the general cargo ship Kaiser left the strait with a cargo while the dry bulk carrier H7Smb8 entered in ballast. This means it will be taking on cargo in the Gulf.

Kpler reported that the Hsin Ocean, which carries refined palm olein in its cargo, entered the strait Tuesday.

On Tuesday, there were no visible VLCCs (very large crude carriers) or LNG (liquefied natural gases) tankers passing through the Strait.

The U.S. Military announced late Tuesday that it had carried out its latest strike on Iran, marking 11 consecutive nights of American attacks.

Two oil tankers?carrying Saudi oil to Asia on Tuesday reversed their course as they headed toward the Bab el-Mandeb strait after?threats by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis who had vowed a?blockade of?Saudi Arabian crude oil shipments moving through the strait

# Wheat rises in 2nd session due to Black Sea supply problems; soybeans and corn firm

Posted to [Maritime Reporter](/blogs/blogs-maritime_reporter)
on
July 22, 2026

Chicago wheat gained ground on Wednesday as attacks on Black Sea grain cargoes, and lower U.S. crop?estimates? from a tour of the U.S. crops underscored concerns over global supplies.

Soybeans, corn and other grains rose in price, tracking the higher crude oil prices, amid rising tensions in Middle East that have reduced global oil supplies.

In a recent note, ING stated that "Disruptions in Black Sea grain imports are not limited to Russia." "Ukrainian imports are also heavily disrupted due to?ongoing Russian assaults on port infrastructure."

Chicago Board of Trade's (CBOT) most active wheat contract rose 0.7% to $6.82-1/2 per bushel at 0256 GMT. This was the second consecutive session of gains. Soybeans gained 0.04% to $12.23-1/4 bushels and corn increased 0.2% to $5.76-1/4 bushels.

In recent weeks, wheat prices have increased after both Ukraine and Russia attacked grain ships and port infrastructure in the Black Sea Sea of Azov.

Wheat prices are also supported by the expectation of lower production. On Tuesday, crop scouts in North Dakota on the first of a three-day annual tour of its hard red spring wheat projected a yield of 46.0 bush

# June U.S. container imports rise 9%, but tariff uncertainty continues to shape trade flows

By   [Jeff Berman](/author/jberman) · July 22, 2026

![June U.S. container imports rise 9%, but tariff uncertainty continues to shape trade flows](https://www.logisticsmgmt.com/images/2025_article/ocean-lm-0625.jpg)

United States-bound June containerized freight shipments saw annual gains for the second straight month, following 12 months of declines, according to data recently issued by S&P Global Market Intelligence.

June imports, at 2.53 million TEU (Twenty-Foot Equivalent Units), posted a 9.0% annual gain, despite the majority of sectors tracked by the firm seeing import declines or slowing growth, while trailing May’s 13.6% annual growth rate. Total second quarter imports rose 5.5% annually, and on a year-to-date basis through June, the firm reported that total imports, at 14.56 million TEU, eked out a 0.9% annual gain.

S&P Global Market Intelligence pointed to a 37.9% annual June gain in consumer discretionary goods, following a 44.1% annual May gain, as the primary growth driver for the month, with those shipments up against weaker annual comparisons, due to weaker 2025 post-tariff shipments, as well as pre-tariff front-loading
